concepts.decision: Model remote, local, co-resident, maintainer, supply-chain, and physical access.
concepts.definition: Attack against behavior around a computation rather than the mathematical design itself.
concepts.failureExample: A system selects a sound algorithm but leaks a key in debug output.
concepts.label: Implementation Attack

concepts.decision: Assess measurable signal, attacker access, repeatability, and secret exposure.
concepts.definition: Leakage via timing, power, electromagnetic signals, cache behavior, or errors.
concepts.failureExample: A co-resident workload observes cache patterns during key operations.
concepts.label: Side Channel

concepts.decision: Use constant-time comparison or equivalent where timing is observable and sensitive.
concepts.failureExample: An authentication check returns faster on the first mismatched byte.
concepts.label: Timing Attack

concepts.decision: Use integrity checks, redundancy, protected boot/update, tamper measures, and physical controls as justified.
concepts.definition: Inducing voltage, clock, memory, input, or environmental faults to alter execution.
concepts.failureExample: A fault makes a device skip secure-boot verification.
concepts.label: Fault Injection

concepts.decision: Normalize external errors, log protected detail, and fail securely.
concepts.definition: Design of failure responses so errors do not reveal secrets or permit unsafe continuation.
concepts.failureExample: Different login errors reveal whether an account, password, or token was valid.
concepts.label: Error Handling

concepts.decision: Use for operations and comparisons exposed to an attacker’s timing measurements.
concepts.definition: Implementation approach that avoids secret-dependent timing where needed.
concepts.failureExample: A compiler optimization reintroduces secret-dependent branch timing.
concepts.label: Constant Time

concepts.decision: Choose when extraction resistance, controlled operations, and physical assurance matter.
concepts.definition: Use of hardware or service boundaries to protect secrets and sensitive operations.
concepts.failureExample: A hardware-backed key is accessible through an enabled debug interface.
concepts.label: Hardware Security

concepts.decision: Apply by facility, device exposure, attacker capability, and consequence.
concepts.definition: Controls limiting physical observation, tampering, maintenance abuse, and device theft.
concepts.failureExample: An unattended device exposes test pads and diagnostic ports.
concepts.label: Physical Security

concepts.decision: Use vetted libraries, review, tests, patching, and controlled changes.
concepts.definition: Engineering practice that avoids unsafe input, state, memory, error, and dependency behavior.
concepts.failureExample: A parser flaw lets malformed input bypass protocol validation.
concepts.label: Secure Coding

misconceptions.claim: Physical controls are irrelevant when cryptography is used.
misconceptions.correction: Physical or local access can enable debug, probing, extraction, or fault paths that undermine an otherwise appropriate cryptographic design.

outcome: Identify timing, side-channel, and fault-injection exposure and select mitigation categories based on the attacker’s observation and access path.

sections.body: Implementation attacks target behavior around a computation rather than defeating the mathematical design directly. A side channel may reveal useful information through timing, power use, electromagnetic emissions, cache effects, error differences, or other measurable behavior. Timing attacks compare response duration or processing path. Fault injection induces or exploits abnormal conditions such as voltage, clock, memory, input, or environmental disturbance to alter execution or extract information. The practical risk depends on the secret, attacker access, repeatability, and measurement quality.
keyPoints: Leakage can be remote, local, or physical depending on the design.
Different error messages and code paths can become observable side channels.
sections.title: Recognize behavior that reveals secrets

sections.body: Use vetted cryptographic implementations and current maintenance processes; avoid data-dependent observable behavior where the threat requires it; use constant-time or equivalent techniques where appropriate; normalize errors; validate inputs; protect secrets in suitable hardware or service boundaries; restrict debug, diagnostic, and physical interfaces; and monitor integrity and configuration. For fault injection, use integrity checks, redundancy or verification where suitable, tamper response, protected boot and update paths, and physical controls proportional to risk. No single defense applies to every platform.
keyPoints: Defenses must match the execution environment and threat capability.
Physical security and secure engineering can be cryptographic controls when they protect implementation behavior.
sections.title: Layer implementation and environmental defenses

sections.body: Define the relevant attacker model before selecting review or testing: remote user, co-resident workload, local maintainer, supply-chain actor, or physical attacker. Review code and configuration, test authorized observable behavior, validate that debug modes and exception paths are disabled or controlled, and assess update and attestation evidence. Treat a patch or compiler change as a potential implementation change; repeat appropriate assurance rather than assuming a mathematical algorithm choice covers the new behavior.
keyPoints: A change in runtime, hardware, compiler, or diagnostic configuration can change leakage risk.
Authorized testing must protect availability and avoid exposing production secrets.
sections.title: Test leakage claims safely and continuously

summary: A sound cryptographic primitive can fail when implementation behavior exposes time, power, electromagnetic, cache, error, or fault information. Implementation attack analysis locates the leakage source, attacker proximity, measurement capability, privilege boundary, and compensating design and operational controls.

assumptions: The boundary is conceptual and does not assert physical isolation.
No scale, exploit probability, or attack success is represented.
Constant-time techniques address relevant timing behavior but do not eliminate every cache, power, error, or fault risk.
teaching.focalRelation: Intended input and output cross the service interface, while timing, errors, cache effects, and power or electromagnetic effects are possible observations; an induced fault travels inward. A possible path is a review target, not proof of leakage or exploitation.

teaching.scenario: A hardware-backed signing service uses an approved algorithm. Remote clients see different error codes and response-duration bands for invalid requests. The service also runs on shared hardware, and technicians can reach a maintenance port. The team has no evidence yet that a secret leaked or that any attack succeeded.
